report:
**Conclusion: The evidence is mixed and overall weak/inconclusive — ginkgo biloba extract may offer modest benefit for some tinnitus patients, but the most rigorous systematic reviews (including Cochrane) do not find reliable, consistent evidence that it relieves tinnitus symptoms better than placebo.**

Details:

- A 2011 systematic review of standardized EGb 761® extract found all eight randomized, placebo-controlled trials favored ginkgo over placebo for tinnitus volume/intensity and global outcomes, concluding it is an "evidence-based" option — but many of these trials had methodological limitations and used a specific, standardized formulation (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3157487/).
- In contrast, a well-cited randomized, placebo-controlled trial combined with a meta-analysis of prior randomized trials (Rejali et al.) concluded that ginkgo biloba does **not** benefit tinnitus patients (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1365-2273.2004.00814.x).
- The Cochrane Collaboration's updated systematic review, considered the highest-quality evidence synthesis, similarly reports no reliable evidence that ginkgo reduces tinnitus severity compared with placebo (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD004407.pub4/full).
- Newer exploratory/open-label studies (e.g., a 2025 uncontrolled study of 170 chronic tinnitus patients on EGb 761®) report symptom improvement, but lack a placebo control, limiting causal conclusions (https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0383/15/1/87).

**Bottom line:** Ginkgo biloba is widely used and generally safe, and some trials—particularly of the standardized EGb 761® formulation—suggest modest symptomatic improvement. However, methodologically stronger randomized controlled trials and the Cochrane review do not confirm a reliable benefit over placebo. Given tinnitus's multifactorial nature, effects likely vary by cause and patient subgroup, so ginkgo should not be considered a proven, reliable treatment for tinnitus relief.
